title: The Smile of the Bell House
premise: Wendell Almeida, a property surveyor hired to appraise Bell House, discovers the house keeps its own ledger: every person who has ever lived there is counted, and the count is due. Waiting on the porch is Pim, the imaginary friend she invented as a child in that very house—unchanged after thirty years, and no longer imaginary. As Wendell races to get the current family out before the house finishes counting them, she learns she was on the original list too, spared only because her parents traded her memory of the truth. In the end Wendell offers herself back to the ledger to erase the family from it, and Pim—the house's memory made flesh—chooses to burn the count instead, leaving Wendell alive but carrying every name the house ever took.
about_author: Vesper Iversen is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade cataloguing condemned properties across New England. They write horror about structures that remember more than the people inside them.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. She arrives at Bell House for a routine estate appraisal, noting its odd symmetry: doors that match windows, rooms that mirror each other. Her instruments give impossible readings—square footage larger inside than out. Emotional beat: professional unease disguised as competence; she tells herself old houses settle strangely.

chapters.title: Doors, Counted
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Following habit, she counts the doors aloud—eleven—and hears a twelfth close somewhere above. The current family, the Okonkwos, are warm and oblivious; their daughter draws a picture of 'the tally man' in the hallway. Beat: dread arrives politely, through small wrongnesses she can explain away.

chapters.title: Pim
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. On the porch at dusk sits a small figure in a yellow raincoat: Pim, her childhood imaginary friend, exactly as she left him thirty years ago. He says only, 'You're late for the count.' Beat: vertigo—the past isn't past, and it's been waiting.

chapters.title: What Mother Signed
chapters.summary: POV Wendell, with a flashback chapter. She calls her mother, who goes silent, then confesses: they lived here when Wendell was six, and something was negotiated to let them leave. Her mother hangs up mid-sentence. Beat: betrayal surfacing—the family she trusted made a trade she can't remember.

chapters.title: The Okonkwo File
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Digging into county records, she finds Bell House has changed hands eleven times; each family stayed roughly seven years, then vanished from local memory—no forwarding addresses, no obituaries. Beat: pattern recognition curdling into horror; the house doesn't lose tenants, it collects them.

chapters.title: Nights Are Inventory
chapters.summary: POV alternating Wendell and Mrs. Okonkwo. Wendell stays overnight to 'finish measurements.' At 3 a.m., footsteps inventory the halls, pausing at each sleeping room. Mrs. Okonkwo wakes feeling counted. Beat: shared dread across two women who don't yet trust each other.

chapters.title: The Room That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Behind the pantry she finds a door she never counted—a twelfth door—opening onto a nursery wallpapered with tally marks, one wall bearing a child's handwriting: WENDELL WAS HERE. Beat: recognition; the house has been keeping her room ready for thirty years.

chapters.title: Pim Explains Nothing
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. She confronts Pim on the porch. He speaks in riddles about ledgers, debts, and 'the arithmetic of staying.' He insists he kept her safe once and can again—for a price. Beat: tenderness twisted by suspicion; is Pim her friend or the house's mouth?

chapters.title: Seven Years, Eleven Families
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. In the county archive she finds a surveyor's logbook from 1931—her own profession, her own handwriting style—describing the same count and ending mid-sentence. Beat: inheritance of doom; this has happened to people like her before, and they failed.

chapters.title: Amara Sees It Too
chapters.summary: POV Amara Okonkwo (age 9). Amara tells Wendell the tally man visits her dreams and asks her to 'hold still.' She shows Wendell where the hallway gets longer at night. Beat: alliance forming between the two who can see; the child's fear is lucid, not hysterical.

chapters.title: The Offer on the Porch
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Pim makes it explicit: the count completes in nine days. One name can be substituted. Bring Wendell back into the ledger, and the Okonkwos go free. Beat: temptation framed as rescue—the price of survival offered in her own currency.

chapters.title: Mother Comes Home
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Her mother arrives unannounced, aged and terrified, carrying the original deed with a signature page that bleeds when touched. She admits what was traded: not money—memory. They sold Wendell's memory of the house to buy her exit. Beat: grief and fury braided together.

chapters.title: Reading the Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. In the nursery, the tally marks rearrange into names under Wendell's touch. She reads the eleven families, then finds her own name struck through with a note: deferred. Beat: the horror of being paperwork; her whole life has been an extension granted, not freedom given.

chapters.title: Trying to Leave
chapters.summary: POV Wendell and Mr. Okonkwo. Wendell urges the family to leave immediately; they pack, but every road out of town loops back to Bell House by mile marker twelve. Beat: futility escalating—the house's jurisdiction is larger than its lot line.

chapters.title: What Pim Is
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Pim finally tells the truth: he is the house's memory given shape, assembled from what Wendell imagined at age six. Every child who lived here made one. The count isn't malice—it's how the house remembers itself. Beat: pity complicating terror; the monster is made of love.

chapters.title: The Twelfth Door Opens
chapters.summary: POV Amara. The tally man enters Amara's dream fully now, and she wakes standing in the nursery, one tally mark already bearing her initial. Wendell finds her there. Beat: point of no return; the count has begun taking names early.

chapters.title: Eight Days Short
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Desperate research reveals the 1931 surveyor tried to cheat the ledger by adding false names; the house took his whole crew instead. Cheating fails. Substitution is allowed. Bargaining is allowed. Beat: strategy narrowing to a single terrible option.

chapters.title: The Negotiation
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. On the porch, Wendell offers herself back—not as substitute prey but as keeper: she will stay, remember everything, and keep the count honest so no family is ever taken again. Pim warns the house may refuse. Beat: courage as bookkeeping; loyalty and truth finally aligned.

chapters.title: The Count Comes Due
chapters.summary: POV all three women in rotation. Midnight: doors open and close in sequence, the house walking itself. The Okonkwos huddle in the kitchen while Wendell stands in the nursery reading names aloud against the rising tally. Beat: climax—memory wielded as resistance.

chapters.title: Pim's Choice
chapters.summary: POV Pim. Given the completed count, Pim must deliver it. Instead he tears the ledger-page of himself—his own tally—from the wall, unmaking the house's memory of its debts. The house screams through every door. Beat: sacrifice; the imaginary friend proves more real than the house.

chapters.title: After the Count
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Dawn. Bell House stands empty and ordinary, its twelfth door bricked over, the Okonkwos driving away with no memory of why they left. Wendell carries the names of eleven families in her head now, vivid as her own. Beat: survival priced and paid; she got everyone out except herself, in a way.

chapters.title: Surveyor's Note
chapters.summary: POV Wendell, epilogue. Months later, Wendell takes a new appraisal job—an ordinary farmhouse—and finds a yellow raincoat folded on its porch rail. She sits down beside it and waits, keeping the lights on, the doors counted. Beat: haunted peace; some friendships survive their houses.
